subject: Culture
title: Translation and Empire
description: A quick win: understand Translation and Empire.

hook.text: When Spanish friars translated 'God' as 'Dios' for the Aztecs, they erased an entire theology of multiple deities.

buildup.text: Colonial translators reshaped indigenous beliefs by forcing foreign concepts into European categories.

discovery.text: The word 'religion' itself has no equivalent in many cultures. Separating sacred from daily life is a Western idea.

twist.text: Missionaries often learned indigenous languages better than anyone. Their dictionaries are now vital for revitalization.

climax.text: Translation can be both a weapon of conquest and a tool of preservation — sometimes simultaneously.

punchline.text: The translator always decides what survives.

quiz.question: Why is the word 'religion' difficult to translate into many indigenous languages?
options: They don't separate sacred from daily life

details.summary: Empires have always used translation strategically — Alexander the Great translated conquered peoples' texts into Greek. The Rosetta Stone enabled British scholars to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs. Colonial translation offices controlled how colonized peoples' words were interpreted.
details.whyItMatters: Translation as imperial tool reveals that controlling how ideas cross language boundaries is a form of political power. The translator's choices shape how conquered cultures are understood.
takeaways: The Rosetta Stone was a colonial artifact enabling imperial knowledge extraction
Colonial translation often deliberately distorted Indigenous concepts
Edward Said's Orientalism exposed how translation constructed the 'East'

faq.question: How did empires use translation as a tool?
faq.answer: Empires translated colonized peoples' texts to understand and control them. Translation offices produced intelligence for administrators. Texts were selectively translated to present colonized cultures as primitive, exotic, or inferior.

faq.question: What is wrong with the Rosetta Stone?
faq.answer: The Rosetta Stone, celebrated as a key to ancient Egyptian writing, was seized by the British from the French, who had taken it from Egypt. It enabled European scholars to decode hieroglyphs — extracting Egyptian knowledge for European use.
